lead: Negative feedback returns a fraction β of the output to the input so that it subtracts from the source. The amplifier gain A falls, but the fall buys a wider bandwidth, steadier gain and less distortion. This is the everyday reason an op-amp circuit with two resistors gives a gain you can trust, even when the transistor inside has a gain spread of 2:1. In a phone charger, an audio preamp or a sensor front end, the same idea sets the gain by resistor ratio β rather than by the active device.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 (common-emitter gain and loading) and Unit 3 (gain-bandwidth product and cut-off frequency). Impedance effects are in 4.2; stability is in 4.3.

blocks.text: The amplifier is a block with open-loop gain A (V/V). The feedback network returns v_f = β v_o to a summing node; β is the feedback factor (V/V). The node subtracts: v_i = v_s − v_f, where v_s is the source and v_i is the amplifier input. The minus sign makes the feedback negative.

blocks.where: A_f is closed-loop gain (V/V); A is open-loop gain (V/V); β is feedback factor (V/V); Aβ is loop gain (dimensionless).

blocks.text: The loop gain is Aβ. The denominator D = 1 + Aβ is the desensitivity. With A = 1000 V/V and β = 0.01 V/V, Aβ = 10, D = 11, and A_f = 1000/11 = 90.9 V/V. The gain has fallen by 11 times.

When Aβ is much greater than 1, A_f ≈ 1/β, so the gain is set by the feedback network. With β = 0.01 V/V, 1/β = 100 V/V. The exact 90.9 V/V is close because Aβ = 10. At Aβ = 3 or 4 the approximation is poor.

D spends the lost gain on stability. A small open-loop change ΔA gives a closed-loop change ΔA_f/A_f = (ΔA/A)/D. The same D reduces the feedback-corrected part of harmonic distortion and noise. Noise already at the input is not reduced.

blocks.where: ΔA/A is the fractional open-loop change; ΔA_f/A_f is the fractional closed-loop change; D = 1 + Aβ.

blocks.text: In the worked example A rises by 10 %. D = 11, so A_f rises by 10 %/11 = 0.91 %. A transistor gain that varies by ±20 % becomes a closed-loop gain that varies by about ±1.8 %. This is why resistor ratios, not transistor spreads, set the gain of an audio preamp.
Distortion works the same way. If the open-loop amplifier adds 8 % THD, the feedback-corrected output distortion is about 8 %/11 = 0.73 %. This applies to distortion generated inside the loop.
Negative feedback raises the upper cut-off and lowers the lower cut-off. The closed-loop bandwidth is BW_f ≈ BW × (1 + Aβ) = BW × D. The gain falls by D, so A_f × BW_f ≈ A × BW.
BW_f = BW (1 + Aβ),   A_f × BW_f ≈ A × BW
blocks.where: BW is open-loop bandwidth (Hz); BW_f is closed-loop bandwidth (Hz).

blocks.text: From the example: BW = 10 kHz, D = 11, so BW_f = 10 kHz × 11 = 110 kHz. The open-loop product is 1000 × 10 kHz = 10⁷ Hz. The closed-loop product is 90.9 × 110 kHz ≈ 10⁷ Hz. The gain falls by 20 log₁₀(11) ≈ 20.8 dB while bandwidth rises by 11.

This is a first-order picture with one dominant pole, as in Unit 3. When β changes the poles move; stability is 4.3. Which impedance rises or falls depends on the feedback topology, not on β alone; see 4.2.

figure.caption: The β network returns 0.01 v_o to the summing node, where it subtracts from v_s. The amplifier sees only v_i, so the loop gain 10 sets the closed-loop gain.

examples.question: An amplifier has open-loop gain A = 1000 V/V and open-loop bandwidth BW = 10 kHz. Negative feedback with β = 0.01 V/V is applied. Find the loop gain and desensitivity. Find the closed-loop gain. Find the closed-loop bandwidth. If A rises by 10 %, find the percentage change in closed-loop gain.
steps: Closed-loop gain: A_f = A/D = 1000/11 = 90.909... V/V, rounded to 90.9 V/V.
Closed-loop bandwidth: BW_f = BW × D = 10 kHz × 11 = 110 kHz.
examples.answer: Aβ = 10, D = 11, A_f = 90.9 V/V, BW_f = 110 kHz, and the closed-loop gain changes by about 0.91 % when A changes by 10 %.
examples.check:
A = 1000.0
BW = 10e3
beta = 0.01
Abeta = A * beta
D = 1 + Abeta
Af = A / D
BWf = BW * D
delta_percent = (0.10 / D) * 100
print(Abeta)
print(D)
print(Af)
print(BWf)
print(delta_percent)

traps: Using A_f = A/(1 − Aβ): negative feedback subtracts, so the denominator is 1 + Aβ. The minus sign belongs to positive feedback (4.4).
Using A_f ≈ 1/β too early: check Aβ. At Aβ = 3 the error is 33 %, at Aβ = 4 it is 25 %.
Writing β = 1 for 1 %: β is a voltage ratio, so 1 % = 0.01 V/V.
Saying feedback raises the gain-bandwidth product: it keeps A_f × BW_f roughly equal to A × BW.
Assuming all impedances fall: the direction depends on the feedback topology (4.2).

quiz.q: Define loop gain and desensitivity for the feedback block diagram.
quiz.a: Loop gain = Aβ, dimensionless. Desensitivity D = 1 + Aβ.

quiz.q: Why does A_f depend mainly on β when Aβ is large?
quiz.a: Because A_f = A/(1+Aβ) ≈ 1/β. The large loop gain makes the exact A cancel.

quiz.q: A = 200 V/V, β = 0.05 V/V. Find Aβ, D and A_f.
A = 500 V/V, BW = 50 kHz, β = 0.02 V/V. Find A_f and BW_f.
An amplifier has A = 100 V/V and β = 0.02 V/V. Is A_f ≈ 1/β acceptable? Show numbers.
quiz.a: Aβ = 2, D = 3, A_f = 33.3 V/V. 1/β = 50 V/V, which is 50 % higher. Not acceptable; Aβ is too small.

quiz.q: Why does the same D reduce distortion but increase bandwidth?
quiz.a: Negative feedback subtracts a scaled output, so it corrects slow variations and distortion by factor D. A dominant pole shifts the cut-off by D, so bandwidth rises by D.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, negative feedback is the default for op-amp, audio and sensor amplifiers because resistor ratios set gain and bandwidth trade. Datasheets give gain-bandwidth product, phase margin and settling time; search those with op-amp stability next. RF designers use less feedback above a few hundred MHz because parasitic capacitance adds phase shift. Control engineers use the same loop gain and desensitivity for motor speed and power-supply regulation.
